newsitem.title: UK: OPTIONS - Euromark volatility falls to find floor.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Euromark volatility falls to find floor.

text.p: Implied volatility of Euromark options traded on LIFFE fell on Tuesday, but traders said the current low levels are unlikely to allow much further downward movement.
A stable rate outlook in Germany has pushed front month volatility down into single figures, which compares with levels of 16 to 17 percent at the start of the year.

German Bundesbank officials have recently said a rate cut was unlikely, and would erode trust in the central bank's policies. Traders said investors believe German economic growth is too low to allow rates to be raised.
"Germany can't afford to hike rates," said Luke White, a broker at Fimat Futures in London. "But volatility, particularly in December is looking exceedingly cheap."

Germany last raised rates in mid-1992, and last cut rates in April 1996. The German Lombard rate is currently at 4.50 percent while the discount rate is 2.50 percent. The repo rate is at 3.0 percent and has not been changed since August 1996.

June options volatility traded as low as 7.0 percent for the 96.75 puts, in a 1,000 lot trade. That was down slightly from 7.25 percent on Monday. However, traders said the approaching expiry was skewing the vol.
June options on the June future expire on June 16. June Euromark futures were trading unchanged at 96.80 by 1300 GMT.
In September options vol was down 0.25 at 8.75 percent, while December was down around the same amount at 12.0 percent.
"It's reached a bit of a floor here," said a trader at a major British brokerage on the LIFFE floor. "Only March seems to be immune to the volatility sell off."
White said December was particularly cheap, since a vol of 12.0 percent infers gamma, the rate of movement in the price of the underlying, of three ticks.
"A daily move of only three ticks up or down could be thrown off track easily, by news or comments," he said. "I'd short March and buy December as a volatility trade."

Notable trades include June 96.75/97.00 strangles, and September/December 97.00 calendar call spreads where the December calls were bought and the September contracts sold. The trade assumes no change in German interest rates.
